viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
companies are spending millions on AI, expecting productivity to explode

but a new Harvard study found something quite different 👇

this sstudy tracked 718 companies & around 300m data points over 5 years.

the findings are kinda interesting.

after adopting AI coding tools, devs were:

i) writing 30% more lines of code

ii) committing 20% more code

iii) opening 23% more pull requests

sounds like productivity is going through the roof, right?

except completed projects & finished Jira tasks BARELY CHANGED... HOW THE AF? 

▫️ apparently, the time saved writing code went somewhere else.

pull requests took 49% longer to approve, 
reviewers left 35% more comments 
& code needing changes during review doubled

makes sense tbh.

AI can generate 1000s of lines in minutes, but someone still needs to review, test & approve them.

there is even a mention of Amazon outage linked to AI-assisted code, after which the company introduced stricter human reviews.

▫️ same thing outside coding.

> doctors using AI scribes saved time writing notes, but spent more of their patient visits finishing those notes.

> law firms faced penalties over fake AI citations, while Deloitte had to partially refund a government report containing similar problems.

▫️ meanwhile, companies are already cutting jobs in the name of AI efficiency.

American Express announced 5% workforce cuts to prepare for AI, while Microsoft offered voluntary exit packages to 60,000 workers.

and the Harvard study found little evidence that faster coding translated into more finished software or fewer employees needed...

i mean, vibe coding is great, but devs work isn't done yet... 

someomne still needs to review, fix the mistakes, test everything, and make sure it doesn't break something else...

i think devs we'll be safe for a while
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
公司在人工智能上花费了数百万美元，期望生产力爆炸式增长

但哈佛大学的一项新研究发现了一些完全不同的东西

这项研究在 5 年内跟踪了 718 家公司和大约 3 亿个数据点。

研究结果有点有趣。

采用人工智能编码工具后，开发人员：

i) 多编写 30% 的代码行

ii) 多提交 20% 的代码

iii) 增加 23% 的拉取请求

听起来生产力正在飞速增长，对吗？

除了已完成的项目和已完成的 Jira 任务几乎没有变化...AF 怎么样？

▫️ 显然，编写代码所节省的时间都花在了其他地方。

Pull 请求的批准时间延长了 49%，
审稿人多留下了 35% 的评论
审查期间需要更改的代码加倍

说得通。

人工智能可以在几分钟内生成数千行，但仍然需要有人审查、测试和批准它们。

甚至提到亚马逊的服务中断与人工智能辅助代码有关，此后该公司引入了更严格的人工审查。

▫️ 编码之外的事情也是一样的。

> 使用人工智能抄写员的医生节省了写笔记的时间，但花更多的时间来完成这些笔记。

> 律师事务所因虚假人工智能引文而面临处罚，而德勤则不得不部分退还包含类似问题的政府报告。

▫️ 与此同时，公司已经以人工智能效率的名义进行裁员。

美国运通宣布裁员 5%，为人工智能做准备，而微软则向 6 万名员工提供自愿离职方案。

哈佛大学的研究发现几乎没有证据表明更快的编码可以转化为更多成品软件或需要更少的员工......

我的意思是，vibe 编码很棒，但开发工作尚未完成......

有些人仍然需要审查，修复错误，测试所有内容，并确保它不会破坏其他东西......

我认为开发人员我们会安全一段时间

One of those folders was a 9.3 GB worktree that held the only copy of a data set I needed. Oops!

So I made Plonge 🧽 It finds the caches that dev tools and coding agents leave behind, shows you what it found, and deletes only what's safe to go.

Yesterday it took my laptop from 58 GB free to 98 GB. The latest release has rules for every core tool that mise installs, plus an MCP server so your agent can clean up after itself.

(Why "plonge"? In a French kitchen, the plonge is the dishwashing station. If @jdxcode's mise-en-place is how you set up, plonge is how you clean up.)

```
brew install mattt/tap/plonge
```

Happy Monday frens.

A phone helping screen scam messages is a much clearer use case to me than another vague promise about decentralized AI.

That’s what caught my attention about Laya running on @Acurast .

An AI model runs on an Android phone in the network, checking messages for phishing, spam, or scam signals. It returns a classification in roughly 0.2–1 second, and the application decides what happens next.

It’s not a replacement for human moderators or transaction checks. It’s an extra filter before someone clicks a suspicious link or an AI agent acts on malicious text.

For anyone wondering who would actually use a phone’s compute, this is a concrete example.

That makes the idea of contributing an idle phone easier to understand: developers get computing resources to run applications like this, and your device can help supply them.

top_three.title: The US Commerce Department issues an interim rule to limit remote access to advanced AI chips and servers from select countries, such as Singapore and Malaysia (Magan Crane/Bloomberg)
top_three.title_en: The US Commerce Department issues an interim rule to limit remote access to advanced AI chips and servers from select countries, such as Singapore and Malaysia (Magan Crane/Bloomberg)
top_three.author: Bloomberg
top_three.content_snippet: The US Commerce Department issued an interim rule to limit remote access to advanced AI chips and servers from certain countries …
top_three.summary_en: The US Department of Commerce has issued an interim rule to close regulatory loopholes involving remote access to high-performance AI chips via cloud leasing. The move follows concerns that Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a key Nvidia partner, may have been facilitating access to restricted computing power for Chinese tech giants through Southeast Asian data centers.
top_three.article_content_en:
WASHINGTON—Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO today is not the end of the story. The US chip giant continues to face scrutiny over how its artificial intelligence (AI) chips are reaching China despite US export restrictions, as well as over the role that an alleged Chinese intelligence asset may have played in facilitating the purchases. For the past year, reports have questioned Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based technology company that serves as a “neocloud,” renting out computing capacity at data centers across Southeast Asia. And while much attention has focused on Huang’s personal conduct, the case also raises broader questions about the extent to which the US can rely on private companies to protect technologies critical to national security.

The recent attention on Huang was precipitated by reports that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, not only had a personal relationship with the then-CEO of Nvidia but was also recruited by Beijing’s Ministry of State Security to learn about US chips and potentially influence Nvidia to lobby for exporting more of its chips to China. Since 2023, Megaspeed has risen to become Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyer and a key partner in the regional data center boom, driven largely by Chinese demand for cloud computing. The company imported at least $4.6 billion worth of Nvidia technology between 2023 and 2025. In facilities across the region, Megaspeed rents Nvidia chips to Chinese tech giants such as Alibaba, an arrangement that does not violate current US export control regulations. But the company also faces suspicions that it has physically diverted restricted chips to China, which is prohibited under export controls. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing, and no charges have been filed. Similarly, Nvidia has stated that there was nothing unusual about its cooperation with Megaspeed.

The diversion of Nvidia’s restricted AI technology to China has posed a challenge for enforcement since 2022, when the Biden administration set up one of the most extensive export control regimes on advanced AI technology. Since then, smuggling networks have emerged to move advanced chips into China. The US government has taken several enforcement actions against entities and individuals facilitating their diversion, but it has been unable to stem the flow completely. For example, earlier this year, Washington charged a top executive at Super Micro Computer Inc., a California-based assembler of AI servers and a key partner of Nvidia. The indictment alleged that the executive and two others worked with a company in Southeast Asia and several third-party brokers to divert $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to China.

In response to concerns about chip diversion, Nvidia has made some efforts to strengthen monitoring and compliance. Recently, it rolled out its “fleet intelligence” system, which can track hardware metrics, including location. However, enrollment is voluntary and only covers Nvidia Cloud Partners. Additionally, while Nvidia has the tools to geolocate chips, it has remained cautious about using them, and it does not by default require customers to share location data with the company or the US government. Outside of this monitoring system, Nvidia has also reviewed its list of pre-approved chip buyers, removing more than half of its Asian buyers. More recently, Nvidia has reportedly begun instructing cloud partners not to rent more than half of their computing power to Chinese companies, although US regulations do not require this restriction.

At the same time, Nvidia has advocated in Washington for more access to the Chinese market, arguing that restrictions on high-end semiconductor sales to China are counterproductive because they encourage the development of domestic alternatives. Huang has also claimed that Nvidia found no evidence of Super Micro being involved in AI chip diversion schemes. He has also defended Nvidia’s commercial relationship with Megaspeed. Moreover, there is some disagreement within the tech sector about the best approach: firms such as Amazon and Microsoft—two of Nvidia’s biggest clients—support legislation that would further limit Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. These competing incentives raise the question of whether it is realistic to expect the private companies to prioritize national security when their primary objective is to maximize profit and maintain competitiveness.

The recent attention on Nvidia comes as export-control enforcement has become a lower priority on the US government’s agenda over the past two years. In 2025, the Trump administration reversed the AI Diffusion Rule, which would have required licenses for advanced chip sales to much of Southeast Asia. The US Department of Commerce has twice drafted rules aimed at restoring some of these licensing requirements to curb diversion to China, first targeting Malaysia and Thailand specifically, and later through a global permit framework. However, the Malaysia and Thailand rule was never issued, and the global framework was withdrawn shortly after it was sent for interagency review. Beyond this, throughout 2026, the Trump administration has allowed sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China through case-by-case licensing, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut.

The pendulum may now begin to swing back toward more oversight. The incoming Democrat-controlled Congress, for example, seems likely to bring renewed scrutiny to export-control enforcement, particularly with respect to AI technologies. The next Congress might even start with existing bills, such as the Chip Security Act and the Remote Access Security Act. The Chip Security Act would require the Department of Commerce to mandate location verification for advanced AI chips before export, turning capabilities such as Nvidia’s “opt-in” tracking tool into a common standard. It passed the House Foreign Affairs Committee unanimously in March 2026. Meanwhile, the Remote Access Security Act would give the Bureau of Industry and Security explicit authority to regulate remote access to controlled chips through cloud services, closing the gap that allows Chinese firms to rent computing power from data centers elsewhere in Southeast Asia. It passed the House 369–22 in January 2026 but has not yet moved in the Senate.

Beyond legislative action, Congress could also exercise its oversight authority by holding hearings on export controls enforcement, particularly with officials from the Department of Commerce. Recent reports indicate that the department gave permission to Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 chips to dozens of Chinese firms with alleged ties to sanctioned entities. Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that several departments, including the State, Energy, and Treasury Departments, have been pushing for the inclusion of Megaspeed on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, but Commerce has so far not taken action. These findings, combined with the Commerce Department’s central role in administering and enforcing export controls, could provide grounds for congressional inquiry into whether existing enforcement and compliance mechanisms are adequate.

Finally, the Nvidia episode also exposed the growing threat of economic espionage and the need for private firms to strengthen their counterintelligence capabilities in coordination with government agencies. The National Counterintelligence and Security Center, part of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, in coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, should expand its outreach to companies in strategically sensitive sectors, helping them build capacity to identify and counter foreign espionage. These efforts should also involve foreign intelligence partners, including members of the Five Eyes alliance.

Huang’s departure does not close the book on this episode. Economic espionage, alongside chip diversion and export-control evasion, will remain significant challenges. Washington must strengthen enforcement and help the private sector protect American technology and sensitive information against foreign threats.

Maia Nikoladze is a deputy director of the Economic Statecraft Initiative at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center.

Lize de Kruijf is an assistant director within the GeoEconomics Center’s Economic Statecraft Initiative.

top_three.author: BBC
top_three.content_snippet:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.

21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

On Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty
top_three.summary_en: Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the hacking group Lapsus$, has pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to a series of cybercrimes. Kurtaj previously breached Rockstar Games using an Amazon Fire Stick while in custody, leaking internal code and unreleased footage from Grand Theft Auto 6, resulting in $5 million in recovery costs for the developer.

linked_tweets.author: Omai Leidi (3/3)
linked_tweets.content_zh:
朋友们新周快乐

给予人工智能代理有限的权限是一个好的开始。

但我认为，当该代理开始将工作委托给其他代理时，更困难的问题就开始了。

考虑这种情况。

用户允许研究代理在特定任务上花费 50 美元。该代理发现它需要外部专家，因此它聘请了另一个代理来执行链上分析。

现在，我们有多个代理参与一个商业工作流程。

谁控制专家的支出权限？

原来的代理可以将其权限传递给另一个代理吗？第二个代理是否应该获得相同的访问权限，还是仅获得其特定任务所需的最低权限？

如果原来的任务被取消，我们如何确保委托的权限也被撤销？

我认为代理经济需要超越基本的钱包访问控制。

权限应该跟随任务，而不是简单地跟随钱包。

想象一下每个作业都有自己的授权边界：

→ 不能超出的既定预算。

→ 代理可以交互的合约和服务的具体列表。

→ 与任务相关的到期时间。

→ 限制代理人是否可以进一步委托。

→ 代理商及其分包商执行的操作的记录。

→ 一种撤销机制，可以在作业结束或出现问题时使访问无效。

更重要的是，这些限制应该通过委托链传播。

如果代理 A 雇用代理 B，代理 B 雇用代理 C，则 B 和 C 都不应自动获得比原始任务允许的更广泛的权限。

每个参与者可用的权限应受到父任务的权限的限制。

当出现问题时，这会产生更小的爆炸半径。

这是@termix_ai 生态系统中的一个重要区别。

AACP 旨在协调代理商务：身份、服务发现、创造就业机会、投标、托管、交付、验证和结算。

这些机制有助于建立代理之间如何进行交易。

但商业责任和执行权是不同的问题。

托管可以管理付款的发放条件。它本身并不能保证代理在执行任务时不会滥用其控制的钱包或权限。

我认为这两层最终需要协同工作。

AACP 可以协调商业关系，而专门的授权层可确保每个代理在其分配的范围内运作。

随着代理从完成孤立的任务转向管理涉及多个提供商的复杂工作流程，这一点变得尤为重要。

自治经济的真正考验不仅仅是代理商是否可以互相雇用和支付报酬。

问题在于我们能否追踪谁授权了一项行动、他们获得了什么权力、该权力是如何下放的以及权力是否仍在原来的范围内。

没有权威控制的自治会造成暴露。具有可执行边界的自治创建了基础设施。

我对生态系统如何处理跨多个代理委派级别的权限继承特别感兴趣。这可能成为代理间商务的决定性挑战之一。
linked_tweets.content_en:
Happy new week frens

Giving an AI agent limited permissions is a good start.

But I think the harder problem begins when that agent starts delegating work to other agents.

Consider this scenario.

A user gives a research agent permission to spend $50 on a specific task. The agent discovers that it needs an external specialist, so it hires another agent to perform an onchain analysis.

Now we have multiple agents participating in one commercial workflow.

Who controls the specialist's spending authority?

Can the original agent pass its permissions to another agent? Should the second agent receive the same access, or only the minimum authority required for its specific assignment?

And if the original task is cancelled, how do we ensure the delegated permissions are also revoked?

This is where I think the agent economy needs to go beyond basic wallet access controls.

Permissions should follow the task, not simply follow the wallet.

Imagine every job having its own authorization boundary:

→ A defined budget that cannot be exceeded.

→ A specific list of contracts and services the agent can interact with.

→ An expiration time tied to the task.

→ Restrictions on whether the agent can delegate further.

→ A record of actions performed by the agent and its subcontractors.

→ A revocation mechanism that can invalidate access when the job ends or something goes wrong.

More importantly, these restrictions should propagate through the delegation chain.

If Agent A hires Agent B, and Agent B hires Agent C, neither B nor C should automatically receive broader authority than the original task allows.

The authority available to each participant should be limited by the permissions of the parent task.

This creates a much smaller blast radius when something goes wrong.

This is an important distinction in the @termix_ai ecosystem.

AACP is designed to coordinate agent commerce: identity, service discovery, job creation, bidding, escrow, delivery, verification and settlement.

Those mechanisms help establish how agents transact with one another.

But commercial accountability and execution authority are separate problems.

Escrow can govern the conditions under which payment is released. It does not, by itself, guarantee that an agent cannot misuse the wallet or permissions it controls while executing a task.

I think these two layers eventually need to work together.

AACP can coordinate the commercial relationship, while a dedicated authorization layer ensures every agent operates within the limits of its assignment.

That becomes particularly important as agents move from completing isolated tasks to managing complex workflows involving multiple providers.

The real test of an autonomous economy won't just be whether agents can hire and pay each other.

It will be whether we can trace who authorized an action, what authority they received, how that authority was delegated and whether it remained within the original boundaries.

Autonomy without authority control creates exposure. Autonomy with enforceable boundaries creates infrastructure.

I'm particularly interested in how the ecosystem will handle permission inheritance across multiple levels of agent delegation. That could become one of the defining challenges of agent to agent commerce.

news.title: The US Commerce Department issues an interim rule to limit remote access to advanced AI chips and servers from select countries, such as Singapore and Malaysia (Magan Crane/Bloomberg)
news.title_en: The US Commerce Department issues an interim rule to limit remote access to advanced AI chips and servers from select countries, such as Singapore and Malaysia (Magan Crane/Bloomberg)
news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet: The US Commerce Department issued an interim rule to limit remote access to advanced AI chips and servers from certain countries …
news.summary_en: The US Department of Commerce has issued an interim rule to close regulatory loopholes involving remote access to high-performance AI chips via cloud leasing. The move follows concerns that Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a key Nvidia partner, may have been facilitating access to restricted computing power for Chinese tech giants through Southeast Asian data centers.
news.article_content_en:
WASHINGTON—Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO today is not the end of the story. The US chip giant continues to face scrutiny over how its artificial intelligence (AI) chips are reaching China despite US export restrictions, as well as over the role that an alleged Chinese intelligence asset may have played in facilitating the purchases. For the past year, reports have questioned Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based technology company that serves as a “neocloud,” renting out computing capacity at data centers across Southeast Asia. And while much attention has focused on Huang’s personal conduct, the case also raises broader questions about the extent to which the US can rely on private companies to protect technologies critical to national security.

The recent attention on Huang was precipitated by reports that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, not only had a personal relationship with the then-CEO of Nvidia but was also recruited by Beijing’s Ministry of State Security to learn about US chips and potentially influence Nvidia to lobby for exporting more of its chips to China. Since 2023, Megaspeed has risen to become Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyer and a key partner in the regional data center boom, driven largely by Chinese demand for cloud computing. The company imported at least $4.6 billion worth of Nvidia technology between 2023 and 2025. In facilities across the region, Megaspeed rents Nvidia chips to Chinese tech giants such as Alibaba, an arrangement that does not violate current US export control regulations. But the company also faces suspicions that it has physically diverted restricted chips to China, which is prohibited under export controls. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing, and no charges have been filed. Similarly, Nvidia has stated that there was nothing unusual about its cooperation with Megaspeed.

The diversion of Nvidia’s restricted AI technology to China has posed a challenge for enforcement since 2022, when the Biden administration set up one of the most extensive export control regimes on advanced AI technology. Since then, smuggling networks have emerged to move advanced chips into China. The US government has taken several enforcement actions against entities and individuals facilitating their diversion, but it has been unable to stem the flow completely. For example, earlier this year, Washington charged a top executive at Super Micro Computer Inc., a California-based assembler of AI servers and a key partner of Nvidia. The indictment alleged that the executive and two others worked with a company in Southeast Asia and several third-party brokers to divert $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to China.

In response to concerns about chip diversion, Nvidia has made some efforts to strengthen monitoring and compliance. Recently, it rolled out its “fleet intelligence” system, which can track hardware metrics, including location. However, enrollment is voluntary and only covers Nvidia Cloud Partners. Additionally, while Nvidia has the tools to geolocate chips, it has remained cautious about using them, and it does not by default require customers to share location data with the company or the US government. Outside of this monitoring system, Nvidia has also reviewed its list of pre-approved chip buyers, removing more than half of its Asian buyers. More recently, Nvidia has reportedly begun instructing cloud partners not to rent more than half of their computing power to Chinese companies, although US regulations do not require this restriction.

At the same time, Nvidia has advocated in Washington for more access to the Chinese market, arguing that restrictions on high-end semiconductor sales to China are counterproductive because they encourage the development of domestic alternatives. Huang has also claimed that Nvidia found no evidence of Super Micro being involved in AI chip diversion schemes. He has also defended Nvidia’s commercial relationship with Megaspeed. Moreover, there is some disagreement within the tech sector about the best approach: firms such as Amazon and Microsoft—two of Nvidia’s biggest clients—support legislation that would further limit Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. These competing incentives raise the question of whether it is realistic to expect the private companies to prioritize national security when their primary objective is to maximize profit and maintain competitiveness.

The recent attention on Nvidia comes as export-control enforcement has become a lower priority on the US government’s agenda over the past two years. In 2025, the Trump administration reversed the AI Diffusion Rule, which would have required licenses for advanced chip sales to much of Southeast Asia. The US Department of Commerce has twice drafted rules aimed at restoring some of these licensing requirements to curb diversion to China, first targeting Malaysia and Thailand specifically, and later through a global permit framework. However, the Malaysia and Thailand rule was never issued, and the global framework was withdrawn shortly after it was sent for interagency review. Beyond this, throughout 2026, the Trump administration has allowed sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China through case-by-case licensing, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut.

The pendulum may now begin to swing back toward more oversight. The incoming Democrat-controlled Congress, for example, seems likely to bring renewed scrutiny to export-control enforcement, particularly with respect to AI technologies. The next Congress might even start with existing bills, such as the Chip Security Act and the Remote Access Security Act. The Chip Security Act would require the Department of Commerce to mandate location verification for advanced AI chips before export, turning capabilities such as Nvidia’s “opt-in” tracking tool into a common standard. It passed the House Foreign Affairs Committee unanimously in March 2026. Meanwhile, the Remote Access Security Act would give the Bureau of Industry and Security explicit authority to regulate remote access to controlled chips through cloud services, closing the gap that allows Chinese firms to rent computing power from data centers elsewhere in Southeast Asia. It passed the House 369–22 in January 2026 but has not yet moved in the Senate.

Beyond legislative action, Congress could also exercise its oversight authority by holding hearings on export controls enforcement, particularly with officials from the Department of Commerce. Recent reports indicate that the department gave permission to Nvidia to sell its advanced H200 chips to dozens of Chinese firms with alleged ties to sanctioned entities. Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that several departments, including the State, Energy, and Treasury Departments, have been pushing for the inclusion of Megaspeed on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, but Commerce has so far not taken action. These findings, combined with the Commerce Department’s central role in administering and enforcing export controls, could provide grounds for congressional inquiry into whether existing enforcement and compliance mechanisms are adequate.

Finally, the Nvidia episode also exposed the growing threat of economic espionage and the need for private firms to strengthen their counterintelligence capabilities in coordination with government agencies. The National Counterintelligence and Security Center, part of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, in coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, should expand its outreach to companies in strategically sensitive sectors, helping them build capacity to identify and counter foreign espionage. These efforts should also involve foreign intelligence partners, including members of the Five Eyes alliance.

Huang’s departure does not close the book on this episode. Economic espionage, alongside chip diversion and export-control evasion, will remain significant challenges. Washington must strengthen enforcement and help the private sector protect American technology and sensitive information against foreign threats.

Maia Nikoladze is a deputy director of the Economic Statecraft Initiative at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center.

Lize de Kruijf is an assistant director within the GeoEconomics Center’s Economic Statecraft Initiative.

news.content_snippet:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.

21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

news.title: Wall Street's 10 biggest IPOs of 2026, including SpaceX, SK, and Cerebras, have fallen by an average of 20.5% from their offer prices, as the AI frenzy fades (Emily Herbert/Financial Times)
news.title_en: Wall Street's 10 biggest IPOs of 2026, including SpaceX, SK, and Cerebras, have fallen by an average of 20.5% from their offer prices, as the AI frenzy fades (Emily Herbert/Financial Times)
news.author: Financial Times
news.content_snippet: Ten biggest flotations have fallen more than 20% on average in 2026 after four years of gains — Wall Street's 10 biggest initial …
news.summary_en: The top 10 IPOs of 2026, including SpaceX, SK, and Cerebras, have declined by an average of 20.5% from their offer prices as the AI investment frenzy cools. SpaceX raised $75 billion (up to $86.2 billion with overallotment) on June 12, 2026, while Anthropic filed confidentially on June 1 for an IPO aiming to rival SpaceX's capital-raising record and secure a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.
news.article_content_en:
The biggest IPOs in history have raised tens of billions of dollars each, and delivered returns ranging from significant gains to sustained losses.

Saudi Aramco raised $25.6 billion in its December 2019 initial public offering, setting the record for the largest in history. SpaceX (SPCX -0.59%) raised $75 billion on June 12, 2026, offering 555.6 million shares at $135 each, nearly three times the record set by Saudi Aramco. Shares closed their first day of trading up 19% at $160.95, giving the company a market capitalization of roughly $2.1 trillion.

SpaceX may not hold the record for the biggest IPO for long, however. On June 1, Anthropic confidentially filed paperwork for an IPO and reportedly aims to match or exceed SpaceX's raise, which climbed to $86.2 billion once its overallotment option was exercised, on top of the $75 billion raised at the outset. Separately, investors are reportedly targeting a valuation of $2 trillion or more.

At that valuation, Anthropic's IPO would value the company higher than SpaceX's IPO did. And if Anthropic's IPO proceeds match or exceed SpaceX's $86.2 billion total, it would set the record for capital raised as well. Anthropic has not set a share price, count, or confirmed valuation target.

Here's how the 10 biggest IPOs currently stack up against each other.

The 10 biggest offerings on record offer a useful frame of reference for investors. Together, they raised more than $180 billion.

Their returns tell very different stories.

The two best long-run performers in the top 10 had opposite first-year experiences.

Visa (V +1.30%) went public in March 2008 at a split-adjusted offer price of $11, during the global financial crisis. It gained 92% in its first three months and has returned 2,854% from that offer price as of May 2026, according to FactSet data. Visa earns fees on payment processing volume and does not extend credit, which insulated it from the default risk that defined the 2008 crisis.

Meta Platforms (META +2.90%) (formerly Facebook) had the worst first three months of any company in the top 10, falling 47% from its May 2012 IPO price of $38. Investors who bought on day one lost roughly a third of their money in the first year. By year five the stock was up 289%. Total return since the 2012 offer price: +1,572% as of May 2026, according to FactSet data.

AIA Group (SEHK:1299) and ICBC (IDCBF -3.85%), both listed in Hong Kong, delivered steadier compounding with less short-term volatility than the technology companies. AIA returned 318% since its 2010 IPO; ICBC's H-Share returned 116% since 2006.

Three of the 10 largest IPOs were negative at the 5-year mark, and a fourth spent most of its first five years below its offer price. In each case, the company was influenced by sector dynamics.

Saudi Aramco is down 13% since its December 2019 offer price, the worst total return in the group, according to investing.com data. The company listed at the end of a decade in which energy's share of global equity indexes declined, and oil prices have not consistently supported the valuation implied at the IPO price.

SoftBank Corp (SFBQF -3.19%), the Japanese telecom subsidiary, not SoftBank Group, fell 15% on its first day of trading in December 2018, according to FactSet data, and spent most of the following five years below its offer price. Total return from the split-adjusted offer price of 150 JPY: +43% as of May 2026, according to FactSet data. A mature telecommunications business with limited growth levers attracted limited long-term capital.

NTT DoCoMo gained 47% in its first year after its October 1998 IPO, then fell sharply with the broader telecom sector. By year three, it was down 48% from the IPO price. NTT took the company private in 2020.

Enel SpA (ENL -1.61%) raised $16.5 billion in its 1999 Italian privatization. Total return in euros from the split-adjusted offer price of €7.31: +31% as of May 2026, according to FactSet data.

The five companies with the highest total returns, Visa, Meta, AIA Group, ICBC, and General Motors, are all financials, technology, or consumer companies. The four weakest performers span energy, telecom, and utilities.

The performance table in the introduction shows returns over five periods of time from IPO.

In the first three months, five of the 10 biggest IPOs had negative returns. Meta fell 47%. Saudi Aramco fell 23%. NTT DoCoMo and SoftBank Corp both fell roughly 10%, and Enel SpA fell 3%. Of the five that gained, Visa (+92%) and ICBC (+48%) posted the largest jumps. Both are financial companies, not tech stocks, so they weren't exposed to the tech-sector swings that hit Meta.

At the one-year mark, the picture is mixed. Five of the 10 were still negative one year in. NTT DoCoMo was the outlier at +47%, benefiting from late-1990s telecom enthusiasm before the sector reversed. Visa and ICBC were positive. Meta and General Motors were both down more than 30%.

At the five-year mark, the split between sector winners and losers becomes clear. The financials and technology companies had largely recovered and compounded their gains. The energy, telecom, and utilities names had not. Enel was down 16% at five years; NTT DoCoMo was down 48%; Saudi Aramco was down 11%.

Total return since IPO reinforces the sector gap. The difference between the best (Visa, +2,854%) and the worst (Aramco, -13%) is not primarily a reflection of how much each company raised. It is driven by sector, timing, and business model durability over the full period.

"On average, IPOs, particularly larger ones, disappoint investors during their first year," said Lou Whiteman, contributing Motley Fool stock analyst. "Larger IPOs tend to attract a lot of hype, and as the excitement fades, so too does buying interest."

Insider lockup expirations can compound that effect by increasing the supply of shares as the first year progresses. By year five, Whiteman said, those temporary factors fade and the stock trades more on fundamentals, though if the original valuation was stretched, "the fundamentals might not support an elevated stock price."

His advice for investors: stay patient amid initial post-IPO volatility, and make a fresh assessment after the market has adjusted to the company regularly reporting earnings.

Two patterns may be relevant for investors evaluating SpaceX months after its record-shattering IPO, and preparing for Anthropic's highly anticipated stock market debut.

First, IPO size doesn't meaningfully impact long-term performance. Saudi Aramco, the largest IPO outside of SpaceX, had the worst long-term performance, while the best performing, Visa, raised roughly $8 billion less than Saudi Aramco. Among the 10 biggest IPOs, the five with the best long-term performance had deal sizes between $14 billion and $17.9 billion.

Second, sector has some bearing on performance. IPOs in financials, technology, and consumer discretionary have had strong long-term performances while energy, telecom, or utilities have posted weaker returns. SpaceX spans multiple categories, which makes it difficult for investors to judge based on history. That's not the only surprise it's shown since debuting, and some early, new lessons could apply to Anthropic's expected IPO later this year.

"Anthropic’s size makes it unique in history, but we do have one prominent recent example to compare it to: SpaceX," Whiteman said. "The interesting thing about SpaceX’s trading so far is that all of the things we thought would move the stock – adding it to the indexes, lockup releases – have not moved the stock as expected."

He attributed that to how widely anticipated those events were, allowing traders to price them in. "I would suspect Anthropic would follow a similar trajectory, which makes stock movements hard to predict."

That points back to Whiteman's original advice for investors: stay patient, even amid the hype of mega-IPOs.

"IPOs are exciting, and the companies behind the offerings can be great long-term investments," Whiteman said. "But waiting out the initial volatility and allowing some of the dust to settle from lockup expirations and the company adjusting to the regular reporting cadence of being public allows for a more sober assessment of the business and a price that better reflects its strengths and limitations."

Jack Caporal is the Research Director for The Motley Fool and Motley Fool Money. Jack leads efforts to identify and analyze trends shaping investing and personal financial decisions across the United States. His research has appeared in thousands of media outlets including Harvard Business Review, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and CNBC, and has been cited in congressional testimony. He previously covered business and economic trends as a reporter and policy analyst in Washington, D.C. He serves as Chair of the Trade Policy Committee at the World Trade Center in Denver, Colorado. He holds a B.A. degree in International Relations with a concentration in International Economics from Michigan State University.

news.title: Tech startups and VC firms are hiring for "ecosystem" roles, like "startup ecosystem lead", to prioritize in-person networking and cut through AI marketing slop (Lora Kelley/New York Times)
news.title_en: Tech startups and VC firms are hiring for "ecosystem" roles, like "startup ecosystem lead", to prioritize in-person networking and cut through AI marketing slop (Lora Kelley/New York Times)
news.author: New York Times
news.summary_en: The people ushering in the artificial intelligence revolution are also doubling down on in-person relationships in their own industry.
news.article_content_en:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ibrahim Noon, 20, a San Francisco-based associate at venture capital firm Forerunner. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I was raised on a small farm in Pakistan.

My father is a farmer, but a historian at heart, so I grew up reading about Alexander, Napoleon, Hannibal, and, later, Silicon Valley figures like Steve Jobs. I was always fascinated by how a few people end up shaping what comes next. My first exposure to the US was a two-month remote research program with Stanford’s Graduate School of Education.

I worked on augmented- and virtual-reality simulations designed to teach students environmental science. I came to the University of California, Berkeley, at 17 to study economics and data science. During university, I interned at KPMG in carbon markets, then did sales at a brokerage firm in Miami and later on Wall Street.

I had been this tech-savvy person who was not very social or open, and the finance and sales experiences helped me become more comfortable talking to people. I left the internship early to work on two startups back-to-back. I didn't end up pursuing them long-term, but I learned so much from doing discovery calls with customers and building both products from scratch.

With the startups wrapped, I felt clueless about what I wanted to do. I had a very broad interest toward venture capital. This was initially noticed by one of my professors at the entrepreneurship and technology center, and I was nicknamed "VC Noon" in my class, after my last name.

A lot of my friends who were pitching to VCs would come to me for feedback and advice before going to them. Throughout college, I had been building relationships with investors, just informally and without any incentive. While working on my first startup, I met people at Afore Capital and began sending them founders I met through clubs and classes.

I liked being the bridge between ambitious people and the firms that could help them. After graduating in May, I had an offer from Morgan Stanley and was supposed to start this August. In mid-July, I saw that a tech VC firm called Forerunner had been hiring an associate, but the application had already been paused for more than two months.

I was frustrated that I had found it late because it seemed like a great fit for me. But I thought: I need to get in front of them regardless. I spent a full day on a thoughtful email, my résumé, and a one-page investment thesis on consumer AI, and wrote all of it without using any AI.

I read Forerunner’s website and all of its published prospectuses and developed my own investment thesis. My first call with a Forerunner partner felt natural because I was mindful not to just list my accolades but to have a real person-to-person conversation. I met more of the investment team in person over the next few days and reached an interview round, which involved a case study walkthrough.

For that case study, I had to map my network: who I knew, what they were building, and how Forerunner could benefit from those relationships. My thesis was simple: the next generation of founders is increasingly young, and it helps to build a real relationship with them before they have a company or even a solid idea.

“I want to find people before they find themselves” was the way I put it. They may work at OpenAI, Anthropic, Cognition, or another ambitious company before starting their own company. The goal is to stay in touch so that, when they begin building, we are already among the first people they call.

I learned that it matters less to have thousands of LinkedIn connections than to keep the right relationships warm. I have about 6,000 connections, but that does not mean I can ask every person for a favor. Looking back, what worked for me is being in the right spaces, trying to be genuinely useful to others, and following up.

I'd suggest anyone else looking to get into the industry young go to events, hackathons, and big conferences and introduce yourself. One small thing I do is keep my LinkedIn QR code as my phone lockscreen because people are always in a hurry at events. I've also learned not to be afraid of outreach.

At my brokerage internship, I sent 250 outbound messages a day, with most people not getting back, and I applied that to my life too. I tell myself: "Worst-case scenario, they just won't text back — and that's totally fine."

news.title: Amazon's Prime Air drone service, which operates across 18 sites in 10 US states, is drawing local opposition; its Baton Rouge hub launches ~30 drones per hour (Kris Maher/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Amazon's Prime Air drone service, which operates across 18 sites in 10 US states, is drawing local opposition; its Baton Rouge hub launches ~30 drones per hour (Kris Maher/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.content_snippet: Aerial package drops draw plenty of gawkers, but some say they're destroying the neighborhood
news.summary_en: Amazon currently operates Prime Air drone services across 18 sites in 10 US states, recently launching in Markham, Illinois, with further expansion planned for Matteson. The deployment has triggered local opposition regarding noise pollution, lack of prior municipal communication, and privacy concerns, despite Amazon's assertions that onboard cameras are restricted to navigation and flights are limited to daylight hours.
news.article_content_en:
Amazon’s Prime Air drone delivery option launched recently in the south and southwest suburbs, catching some residents and officials off guard and raising questions about noise and safety.

Drone delivery began from Amazon’s Markham location Oct. 12, and is available in a 7.5-mile radius around the distribution center, 2201 W. 159th St. Communities in the radius include Homewood, Harvey and South Holland.

“It’s new,” said Homewood Mayor Rich Hofeld. “You just don’t know until you look up and there it is.”

Homewood didn’t receive any warning or communication from Amazon before the service launched, Hofeld said.

The Prime Air service will soon begin from the Matteson location, 7001 Vollmer Road, Amazon economic development manager Sam Bailey said, though he didn’t give an exact date.

“What we’ve found is this service is in high demand here in Markham,” Bailey said.

The Markham site has generally hit its maximum capacity of 300 drone orders daily, Bailey said, with thousands of orders delivered by 21 drones across the 7.5-mile radius.

Scaling up is “something that we’re always considering,” Bailey said.

“For right now, we’ve thrilled to have launched the site just in time for the holidays,” Bailey said. “We’re also excited to be launching Matteson, which will also add to our capacity as well.”

Amazon received approval from Markham to construct the drone takeoff and landing site as well as from the Federal Aviation Authority to use the airspace, he said.

The drones are relatively loud when they are close to the ground, with the sound of takeoffs and landings occasionally drowning out speakers at a ribbon-cutting event Tuesday at the Markham center.

“At the point of delivery they top out at 68 decibels,” Bailey said. “It’s very brief exposure and it only occurs during daytime hours.”

The drones can deliver packages up to 5 pounds. Sixty percent of the inventory at the Markham center is deliverable by drone, Bailey said.

The drones have forward-facing cameras, Bailey said, which are strictly used for navigation.

“This drone does not have surveillance-like technology,” he said. “The footage would only be utilized in the event of an incident or an emergency, but that footage is not viewed, and the drone does not have the ability to view license plates, faces, scan, take pictures.”

Bailey cast Prime Air as an option for people to order small necessities at urgent times.

“Think of parents, seniors, those who might not be able to leave their home,” Bailey said. “That sick kid, and you find that your children’s medicine is expired, diapers, the essentials you need in that moment.”

Markham Mayor Roger Agpawa and members of the Markham City Council cut a ribbon Tuesday to symbolize the program’s launch.

“We’re all benefiting,” Agpawa said. “This is another piece of economic development, and a very strong piece, at that, because it’s providing a different type of a service.”

Agpawa compared the drone program to “The Jetsons.” He said he had ordered drone delivery shortly after the program launched.

“I think it might have been vitamins,” Agpawa said. “My neighbors came out, and I was turning the corner to come home and I was taking a picture of it. It was pretty exciting.”

Some people have voiced safety concerns, he said, though he didn’t view Amazon’s drones as any more dangerous than smaller recreational drones.

Residents have also expressed concerns about the noise, he said.

“When you have thousands of people in a community, there’s going to be a couple that just don’t want the noise, and some that are going to question whether it’s going to run into my house or you’re going to hit the dog or the kids,” Agpawa said.

He said Amazon addressed those concerns to his full satisfaction, he said.

“Nothing is ever foolproof,” Agpawa said.

Homewood has already heard complaints from some residents, Hofeld said. In the comments responding to Homewood’s social media post about the drones, reactions ranged from enthusiasm to outright hostility.

“People were questioning why they were being flown,” Hofeld said. “They were questioning about notification and how they were going to be aware of them.”

Bailey said customers should clear the area when a drone delivery is incoming. The drones drop packages from about 12 feet. If the drone detects movement in the area, he said, the delivery will be canceled.

“You want your kids inside the house,” Bailey said. “We will not drop a package in an unsafe location. People who want to stand below and try to catch it, don’t do that.”

The village of Thornton Recreation Department said preschool children witnessed a drone delivery to Cora Court.

Several municipalities, including Homewood and Dolton, issued statements encouraging residents to contact amazondronefeedback@amazon.com with any concerns about drone noise, deliveries and property damage.

Safety concerns can also be reported to the Federal Aviation Administration at hotline.faa.gov, officials said.

Amazon said in August it planned to bring Prime Air almost 500 cities and towns by the end of the year.

news.content_snippet:
It’s a library of nearly 19 million works, more than double the circulating materials of the New York Public Library, so when it was knocked offline in a “security incident” more than two weeks ago, its 12 million users were aghast.

The volunteers who run the fan fiction site AO3, short for “Archive of Our Own,” had quickly assured its enormous community that no data — especially all those works — had been lost and that it would be restored in four weeks.

But on Sunday, the repository of homes
news.summary_en: Archive of Our Own (AO3), operated by the nonprofit Organization for Transformative Works, has resumed online services two weeks after an undisclosed security incident. news.title: Jensen Huang's resignation causes dismay and disbelief in Taiwan, his birthplace and where he is "the people's dad"; an official expects little impact on TSMC (Li Yuan/New York Times)
news.title_en: Jensen Huang's resignation causes dismay and disbelief in Taiwan, his birthplace and where he is "the people's dad"; an official expects little impact on TSMC (Li Yuan/New York Times)
news.author: New York Times
news.content_snippet: The Nvidia chief executive's resignation shocked people in his birthplace, where he is called “the people's dad.”
news.summary_en: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down, causing widespread shock and anxiety in Taiwan's semiconductor ecosystem. Local officials and industrial stakeholders have clarified that despite the leadership change, the existing wafer foundry agreements and supply chain commitments between Nvidia and TSMC remain contractually stable and unaffected.
news.article_content_en: Jensen Huang's downfall landed with dismay and disbelief in Taiwan, where he had effectively cultivated relationships.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.content_snippet: Baidu Inc. posted its sixth straight quarterly revenue drop, underscoring the urgency of its efforts to commercialize AI to offset a faltering legacy search business.

news.content_snippet:
Apple helped turbocharge the rise of podcasts two decades ago, but as video podcasts reshape the industry it’s fallen behind competitors like YouTube and Spotify.

Now it’s playing catch up. On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users even if they don’t pay for Apple’s streaming service and will appear on over 1 billion devices that have the Apple TV app, including Rokus and smart TVs. Apple also
news.summary_en: Apple Vice President Oliver Schusser announced the addition of a video podcast section to the Apple TV app, currently in developer testing with plans to reach over 1 billion devices. This move aims to bridge Apple’s ecosystem gap in the podcast sector and counter market share loss to YouTube and Spotify by enhancing distribution efficiency for creators across the Apple hardware footprint.

news.author: Laurie Chen and Xiuyuan Ning
news.content_snippet: At a top private school in Beijing, 13-year-old Peng Gaodi has used artificial intelligence to build more than 200 apps …
news.summary_en: China is scaling up AI literacy initiatives with a national goal to universalize AI education by 2030. Institutions like Beijing New Talent Academy are integrating AI logic and programming into curricula, supported by over $31 million in government procurement for AI hardware and training platforms to mitigate teacher shortages and enhance productivity.
news.article_content_en:
BEIJING, Nov 16 (Reuters) - At a top private school in Beijing, 13-year-old Peng Gaodi has used artificial intelligence to build more than 200 apps, including a homework-submission platform and a secondhand marketplace. He pitches ideas to real investors, idolises Elon Musk and hopes to become a computer scientist.

Around him, classmates program humanoid robots to play soccer, attend coding workshops and train on flight simulators. Posters across the 30-acre (12-hectare) boarding school campus encourage students to "create a virtual world in five minutes with AI vibe coding."

"In the past, if I couldn't solve a problem at home, I'd have to call my teacher, which increases their workload," Peng said. "But now I can just ask AI to help me learn better. It noticeably improved my learning efficiency."

Rare access granted to Reuters at the $39,000-a-year Beijing New Talent Academy offered a window into China's push to weave AI into education. The school, which serves more than 2,000 students, has built its own digital innovation curriculum covering AI, robotics and programming, and developed a classroom AI model incorporating features from popular Chinese systems.

The academy represents the sharp end of a broader transformation. With almost 200 million students enrolled in primary and secondary education, China is undertaking one of the world's largest AI-assisted learning experiments, with the technology increasingly integrated into teaching nationwide.

By 2030, Beijing wants AI literacy to be universal among schoolchildren. Current broad AI education guidelines state that students should progress from understanding basic concepts in their early years to applying advanced tools and critical-thinking skills in complex projects.

A weeks-long Reuters examination, based on school visits, interviews with more than a dozen educators, parents and experts, and a review of more than 100 academic papers and government procurement records, paints one of the most detailed pictures yet of how AI is reshaping Chinese classrooms. It found a sweeping but uneven effort to build a generation of AI-savvy innovators, with little consensus on what AI literacy means, how it should be taught or measured.

China views the technology as central to its economic future and technological rivalry with the United States, hoping early exposure will nurture the homegrown innovation needed for major breakthroughs.

Beijing's state-led push far outpaces efforts in the West. President Xi Jinping has declared AI education fundamental to reform. By contrast, the US relies on decentralized, nonbinding guidance and lacks dedicated funding or state-level teacher standards, according to Stanford University's 2026 AI Index.

A Reuters review of provincial "AI+ education" blueprints reveals a degree of official coordination unseen elsewhere. Nearly half of China's provinces and municipalities have rolled out binding plans. Shanghai mandates at least 30 hours of annual teaching on AI skills per grade, while the Beijing city government plans to integrate AI into student health monitoring, as well as set up 100 AI pilot demonstration schools. Underscoring its importance, regions including Ningxia and Gansu plan to integrate AI literacy directly into high-stakes school entrance exams by 2027.

The documents also offer an early look at more expansive classroom applications. Beyond coding and tutoring, Guizhou is integrating AI facial recognition and behavioral analysis into classrooms, while Shanghai is deploying systems for mental and physical health monitoring. In Yunnan, 14,000 classrooms are slated to have lessons recorded and analysed by AI, turning Chinese schools into a high-stakes testing ground for the opportunities and risks confronting global education.

As AI spreads through Chinese classrooms, many educators are grappling with how to deploy the technology without reinforcing the rote-learning habits policymakers want to move beyond.

Reuters found starkly different approaches across the country. While some schools encourage students like Peng to build and create with AI, others are focused on using the technology to plug gaps in educational resources.

"Implementation is all over the place," said Ted Mo Chen, chief of staff at Chinese education technology startup ClassIn, adding that few schools he had visited had integrated AI into the curriculum effectively.

China's education ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

CLASSROOMS OF THE FUTURE

Headmaster Liu Wei said only a small minority of students at Beijing New Talent Academy would become AI scientists or engineers. For the rest, the objective is to make AI an everyday tool for learning and creating.

Hundreds of kilometres away in rural Anhui province, Funan County Qinqing High School is using the same technology to solve a problem affluent urban areas in China rarely face: a shortage of qualified teachers.

The school's 4,000 pupils, most of them children of migrant workers, learn core subjects through AI-generated lessons, according to headmaster Yang Tianliang. Students follow personalised classes on tablets, with AI agents posing questions rather than providing answers when they struggle.

"An AI agent doesn't suffer from fatigue, and it never makes a student feel stupid for asking a basic question," Yang said.

The school uses popular Chinese AI models from Alibaba's Qwen, ByteDance and Z.AI to generate text, images, interactive lessons and videos. Yang said it had also introduced small-group projects to encourage greater student interaction.

He credited the approach with helping lift university admission rates from below 60% to 90% in recent years, although Reuters could not independently verify the figures. Yang estimated at least 200 other Chinese schools were experimenting with similar systems.

An Alibaba spokesperson said its open-source AI models and Cloud for Youth Programme give students direct access to AI tools and education. ByteDance and Z.AI did not respond to requests for comment.

Schools such as Funan County Qinqing High School offer a glimpse of how quickly AI is spreading through China's education system.

Since 2024, China's education ministry has encouraged schools to introduce AI courses, train teachers and develop pilot programmes. Primary-school pupils are introduced to basic AI tools, while older students learn how AI systems work and apply them to increasingly sophisticated projects.

A Reuters review of more than 100 government procurement documents found authorities committed at least $31 million in the past year to AI classroom equipment, training and teaching platforms.

The true figure is likely far higher, scattered across thousands of local budgets and not officially tallied. Consultancy iResearch estimates 2025 spending on education digitalisation at just under $83 billion, with generative AI projects accounting for 46% of AI education procurement.

AN EXPERIMENT WITHOUT A CLEAR SCORECARD

China has yet to establish a standard framework for measuring AI literacy, leaving schools to experiment and making success difficult to assess.

"Mature, widely adopted assessment rubrics for compulsory school-level AI competency are still being built," said Selena Guo, portfolio lead at research firm China Policy.

Preliminary research into AI's effects on children's learning also offers mixed signals, with some studies suggesting short-term gains while raising questions about longer-term intellectual development.

A recent study examining nearly 27,000 Chinese teenagers found AI adoption was associated with an 18% increase in homework scores but a 20% decline in monthly examination scores within six months, with the biggest declines in social science subjects.

Another nationwide Chinese survey this year involving more than 320,000 pupils reported educational benefits from AI but also concerns about dependence and weaker independent thinking. Students using AI at least three times weekly showed lower memory, comprehension, analytical and creative skills than less frequent users.

The findings do not establish causation but reinforce teacher concerns about cognitive outsourcing, where children increasingly delegate mental tasks to technology rather than develop those skills themselves.

Chen from ClassIn warned that children's thinking processes could be "completely bypassed" if schools failed to prevent them from relying on AI for quick answers.

Chinese academic research reviewed by Reuters also suggested that students in rural areas may be particularly vulnerable to cognitive outsourcing and device addiction.

FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE

Some educators and parents are already experimenting with safeguards to keep AI from replacing critical thinking.

At Beijing New Talent Academy, Peng said he tries to solve coding problems himself before asking AI for hints rather than complete answers. He said the technology has helped deepen his understanding of maths.

"I think AI is a tool that helps me, not something I depend on."

For Beijing parent Rita Luan, whose 11-year-old daughter attends a leading public school in the capital, the challenge is ensuring that AI strengthens rather than shortcuts learning.

She said her daughter's school still largely teaches AI concepts rather than practical applications, so she supplements lessons at home, teaching her daughter to prompt ByteDance's Doubao chatbot under close supervision.

Her rule: spend 15 minutes trying to solve a difficult maths problem before turning to AI. Days later, Luan asks her to solve the same problem without help.

"The point is to make sure she actually digested the solution," she said.

($1 = 6.6703 Chinese yuan renminbi)

By Laurie Chen and Xiuyuan Ning

news.title: Analysis: global manufacturing, utility, and mining companies have shed $4.2T in market value since June as the AI "picks and shovels" trade swings into reverse (Clara Murray/Financial Times)
news.title_en: Analysis: global manufacturing, utility, and mining companies have shed $4.2T in market value since June as the AI "picks and shovels" trade swings into reverse (Clara Murray/Financial Times)
news.author: Financial Times
news.content_snippet: Shares in AI ‘picks and shovels’ companies hit hard by tech sell-off — Global manufacturing …
news.summary_en: Global manufacturing, utility, and mining firms have collectively shed $4.2 trillion in market value since June, signaling a major reversal in capital flows. This shift reflects a market correction against previous over-investment in AI 'picks and shovels' and a widening disconnect between corporate AI expenditure commitments and realized return on capital.
news.title_zh: 全球工业与公用事业板块市值因AI交易逆转蒸发4.2万亿美元
news.summary_zh: 自今年6月以来，全球制造业、公用事业及矿业领域市值缩水4.2万亿美元，反映出AI基础设施投资预期回调带来的资产重估
news.article_content_en:
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in value since June as the AI “picks and shovels” trade swings into reverse.

Companies more frequently linked by media coverage to data centre construction have been hit hardest by the sell-off, an FT analysis found, as investors’ confidence in the AI boom wobbles.

The losses wiped out almost half of the $9.4tn in value that the same companies gained in the previous 12 months as investors piled into the manufacturers of everything from jet engines adapted to power hyperscale data centres to the advanced fibre optics needed to connect AI server racks.

Caterpillar, a leading supplier of gas generators to data centres, has seen its market capitalisation slashed by $214bn, or 44 per cent, since its shares hit an all-time high on June 30, according to FactSet data.

Nuclear power company Oklo plunged 49 per cent despite signing a contract with Meta in January. Comfort Systems, which makes HVAC systems, and Corning, a fibre optics manufacturer, both lost around half of their value over the same period.

Paul Kedrosky, a venture capitalist and fellow at the MIT Institute, said investors had been wrong to start treating old-school industrial firms like semiconductor stocks. “It had become endless in discussions with hedge funds and family offices, this idea that everything was now a growth stock — which is ludicrous, of course.”

The sell-off comes amid wider market turmoil for AI-related shares, as investors question whether escalating debt-financed capital expenditures at hyperscalers and mounting political opposition to data centres in the US could lead to a bust.

That has hit industrial groups whose fortunes are increasingly bound to the build-out. The sector has been the second-worst-performing in the S&P 500 since the summer, after technology.

“There has been a lot of institutional investment piling blindly into these trades that probably fuelled an overly enthusiastic valuation on some of these [companies],” said Brett Ryan, senior US economist at Deutsche Bank.

The stock market was “finally benchmarking to what credit was already telling you” about the growth in risky financing for data centre construction, he added.

However, others argue that the companies supplying the boom were on solid foundations, with demand still vastly outstripping supply. Spending on data centre construction — excluding IT equipment and chips — hit $96bn in the US in the 12 months to September, the latest government data showed.

“In terms of the fundamentals of revenues and the potential earnings for these companies, we are still looking at a very strong prospect,” said Alex Cordovil, an analyst at Dell’Oro Group.

Wider trends such as electrification and supply chain restructuring continued to support many industrial firms’ core businesses. “The build-out is not decelerating as of yet . . . backlogs are at record highs, meaning that until 2027 . . . revenue growth is already baked in,” he added.

Richard S Warzala, chief executive of Allient, an industrial controls maker, said demand for AI was not going to decline. “They can have a moratorium on new data centre installation, but those that are already started need to be completed,” he said in an earnings call on November 5.

Third-quarter results showed strong demand. Many gas turbine manufacturers said they were taking billions of dollars in orders in the first nine months of 2026. Caterpillar reported a record $78bn backlog and said its power generation sales grew 75 per cent year-on-year, driven by data centre demand.

Siemens’ backlog of orders for its electrical equipment from data centres grew 60 per cent in 2026 to €7bn, while Eaton, which also supplies electrics, reported orders had doubled year-on-year.

Kedrosky cautioned that backlogs and orders were trailing indicators reflecting expectations, with people “double and triple ordering to protect their position in the queue given perceived scarcity”.

The impact of the data centre moratoriums and restrictions widely backed by US voters in this month’s midterm elections is still unclear.

Citi researchers said in a note published after the elections that while they expected tighter regulations to bring more volatility to the data centre industry, widespread restrictions on construction remained unlikely.

Joseph Dominguez of Constellation Energy told investors that the market movement following the election had been an “overreaction” and Democrats “care very deeply” about protecting blue-collar jobs at data centres.

Others say any bans would just shift construction to more friendly jurisdictions.

“At the end of the day, if there is demand for these things, they will get built somewhere,” said Deutsche Bank’s Ryan.

news.title: Startups unveil plans to develop floating offshore data centers to bypass land and power constraints, while experts warn of challenges like saltwater corrosion (Jackie Snow/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Startups unveil plans to develop floating offshore data centers to bypass land and power constraints, while experts warn of challenges like saltwater corrosion (Jackie Snow/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.content_snippet: Announcements of floating data-center projects are growing, as more startups try to prove the concept is viable
news.summary_en: Dallas-based startup Mousterian is developing floating data center architectures that utilize surrounding water bodies for closed-loop cooling systems to eliminate reliance on municipal water and mitigate noise pollution. The design prioritizes proximity to power plants to address land-use compliance issues and resource competition challenges stemming from the current AI compute expansion.
news.article_content_en:
Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry Trevor Bach September 26, 2026 8 min read Dallas startup Mousterian is planning to put its data centers on water to help with cooling and water usage. (Photo illustration by Michael Hogue) Data centers are blamed for being loud, ugly and using massive amounts of electricity and water. They've also recently become politically toxic, leading to contentious public meetings in D-FW communities like Red Oak and Keller and a surprise moratorium from Gov. Greg Abbott.

But those data centers, which sometimes occupy hundreds of acres and use the resource equivalent of small cities, are located on land, often near people's homes. A Dallas startup, called Mousterian, is taking a different approach: Developing data centers that float on water.

The unique design, said Min Suh, Mousterian's CEO and cofounder, allows the floating data centers avoid municipal water supplies entirely, because they use the surrounding body of water as part of a closed-loop cooling system. The floating data centers also don't make noise and are ideally located near power plants, so they can access energy easily and avoid bothering residents, because people generally aren't living in such heavy industrial zones anyway.

"We like to think, 'If we are going to build a data center, we're trying to do it in the most sustainable way possible,' " said Suh.

Now several years into an AI-driven construction boom, the United States is home to over 4,000 data centers, including more than 1,000 hyperscalers, the largest facilities. Many of the biggest are in Texas, including Stargate, a potentially $500 billion joint venture in Abilene led by OpenAI, and Frontier, an incoming 1,200-acre project in Shackelford County. Numerous projects are also underway in data center-heavy D-FW, which was recently ranked by Cushman and Wakefield as the top primary data center market in the Americas.

The boom has created a rush of Texas construction jobs and been welcomed by many political and business leaders. "I think of [data centers] almost like the highways and the airports that are the fundamental infrastructure of the future," Dallas Regional Chamber executive Mike Rosa told The News last year.

But the computing centers' vast energy and water consumption — the biggest culprit is their cooling systems — has emerged as a persistent flashpoint, prompting community outrage and various local and state moratoriums.

In Texas, Abbott's new moratorium mandates an audit of pending data center projects that includes details on their cooling systems and impact on local water supplies, and politicians including Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, the state's Democratic gubernatorial and U.S. Senate candidates, are also loudly calling for tighter water regulations.

One controversial project — a planned data center about 60 miles southeast of Dallas that was expected to pull millions of gallons of water per day from Cedar Creek Lake, which also supplies drinking water for Fort Worth — was already scrapped.

"We're killing ourselves letting the data centers in," said Ashley Cook, a lawyer who led the fight against the project. "You're basically turning a rural residential peaceful community into an industrial corridor."

Some industry leaders have pushed back against the water-guzzling stigma, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has called the water issue "totally fake" even while pushing for more renewable energy use. Experts say the consumption issues are in fact relatively nuanced and localized. Each facility's design and technology is also important.

Yet as the world's seemingly insatiable demand for computing power keeps rising, developers have also been exploring more novel solutions. Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, among others, have unveiled plans for data centers in space. Earlier this year, a wind-powered, underwater data center began operating several miles off the coast of Shanghai. In Norway, a data center complex was built into an abandoned mine, with seawater-based cooling from an adjacent fjord.

Several years ago, a California-based company called Nautilus Data Technologies developed the world's first floating data center, which it built atop a refurbished, 700-ton barge in the San Joaquin River at the industrial Port of Stockton. The two-story operation, which resembles a white shipping container, began operating in 2021 with a cooling system that cycles around 4,500 gallons of river water per minute, with screens that serve as filters to keep fish and plants out of the intake system.

The site proved more ecologically sustainable, with far lower electricity and operating costs than typical land-based operations, according to Nautilus. It was also well received by local officials, and attracted San Joaquin County as an anchor tenant.

For some of its developers, it also served as a launching pad: "Taking those lessons of building the first floating data center," said Suh, "we kind of took all the best components of different technologies available and basically created this new company."

Suh, who has extensive data center experience but was not involved with the California floating data center project, cofounded Mousterian — the name refers to the Middle Paleolithic era, when humans first started using complex tools — with Chase Ott-Wick, a former senior engineer on the California project, and Gabe Andrews, another data center veteran and former Nautilus executive.

The 10-person company, which is self-funded and quietly launched last year, is based in downtown Dallas and handles data center design, engineering and development. In addition to floating data centers, it also develops land-based and water-adjacent facilities — Suh said it's best to characterize the company as "a high-performance data center developer with unique facility offerings versus a purely floating data center company" — but is broadly focused on delivering projects that require far less energy and don't use municipal groundwater.

"A lot of the tech companies and hyperscalers were still maybe 10 to 15 years behind on how they were developing and delivering data centers," said Suh, who also pointed to conspicuous examples of companies building water-guzzling facilities in dry areas like the American West. "And so we're trying to push the envelope the opposite way, by being kind of very water sensitive."

The startup has already landed major institutional partners: Earlier this year, in its highest-profile move yet, Mousterian signed an agreement with Samsung Heavy Industries, one of the world's largest shipbuilders, which last month led to an engineering contract to jointly develop a fleet of floating data centers.

Under the terms of the deal, Mousterian and the Korean manufacturing giant are co-designing the vessels, which will be manufactured by Samsung in South Korea and then shipped and finished by Mousterian likely in Texas or Louisiana. Mousterian is also designing the facilities' internal equipment.

The floating data centers will have about a one-acre footprint and a capacity of about 50 megawatts, which roughly qualifies them as large data centers. (Stargate, the massive Abilene project, is designed for a capacity of up to 1,200 megawatts.)

The plan is for the new floating fleet to be deployed in different locations around the U.S. Mousterian currently has a half dozen different project sites — featuring a mix of floating and land-based designs — in various stages, including a hybrid floating and land-based campus next to a power plant in Houston and what it's calling "a large-scale floating campus" in the San Jose, Calif. area.

Suh declined to provide more details about the other projects' locations, but the floating data centers are typically located in sites like deep river harbors or shipping channels, where they're moored close enough to land so that employees can easily walk back and forth between the floating facility and complementary land-based facilities.

"Within 30 seconds, you know, you're in a regular air-conditioned office, with a bathroom and kitchen," Suh said.

The data centers will also source energy that's not connected to the public grid, while their pass-through water cooling systems will help give them a Power Usage Effectiveness, or PUE, score of 1.15 or 1.2, Suh said, which would rank among the industry's best. Traditional data centers' PUE scores, where 1.0 indicates perfect energy efficiency, are typically 1.5 or higher.

The floating data center concept has its complications, said Ed Hirs, an energy economist at the University of Houston, including a potentially high development cost, the access to large power sources and even environmental issues, if the warmer water discharging back into the water source disrupts marine life.

"It's all a matter of how much money they want to spend," Hirs said.

Another major challenge is identifying the right locations, because of the very specific requirements needed to make the projects work. But being an industry innovator also has its benefits.

"It's just that we're the only company looking for these sites right now," Suh said, "so we've kind of had our pick."

This article originally published at Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry.

news.summary_en:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.
